headline: Amazon's careers copy centers on customer obsession, high-bar performance, and scale-driven invention — with DEI language that surged in 2017–18 and has since narrowed.
identity: Amazon has consistently valued customer obsession, high-performance standards, and a builder/inventor identity across nearly two decades of careers copy, with phrases like 'Earth's most customer-centric company' and 'relentlessly high standards' appearing from 2007 through 2026. Altruism and community-outreach language spiked sharply in 2017–18 (z-scores of ~1.54, driven by 'Black to the Future' events, affinity-group outreach, and STEM pipeline programs) but retreated to near-baseline by 2019–2021, suggesting that burst was a distinct content campaign rather than a durable shift. DEI language followed a similar arc: explicit demographic terms like 'LGBTQ,' 'disability,' and 'Black' appeared only in 2017–18, then dropped out; 'diversity,' 'equity,' and 'inclusion' persisted through 2024 but in a compressed, aspirational-vague register, while 2025–26 copy pivots toward 'representation' and workforce-data framing tied instrumentally to customer outcomes.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are driven by ownership and results under pressure — the copy consistently reaches for people who 'rise to the occasion and never settle,' who treat 'success measured against the possible, not the probable,' and who are comfortable being 'misunderstood for long periods of time' while pursuing bold bets.

sections.heading: The Unchanging Core: Customer Obsession and High Standards
sections.body:
From the earliest archived copy in 2007 ('Customer Obsession: We start with the customer and work backwards') through 2026 ('United by our peculiar culture of curiosity, bold ownership and fearless initiative, we channel our customer obsession into making everyday impact'), the careers pages return to the same cluster of ideas: customer-centricity, a high hiring bar, frugality, and invention. Performance-language z-scores are consistently above zero in years with rich data (2007: +0.80; 2011: +1.12; 2016: +1.76), and meritocracy scores track closely alongside them. The Leadership Principles — 'Insist on the Highest Standards,' 'Hire and Develop the Best,' 'Bias for Action' — appear verbatim across multiple years, giving the copy an unusually stable doctrinal quality.

The 2014 data is thin (only 2–3 chunks, flagged as sparse), so that year's apparent dip in most scores should be read cautiously rather than as a real shift.

sections.heading: The 2017–18 Altruism and DEI Peak — and Its Retreat
sections.body:
The most pronounced departure from baseline came in 2017 and 2018, when the careers pages expanded dramatically in volume (131–139 chunks versus 6–45 in adjacent years) and introduced content that scored well above peers on both altruism (z ≈ +1.54) and inclusion (z ≈ +1.54 in 2017; inclusion topk mean of 0.546). Quoted passages described the 'Black to the Future' hackathon, affinity groups (Black Employee Network, Latinos@Amazon, Glamazon), STEM pipeline programs for girls, and pay-equity commitments. The DEI register in 2017 included 25 chunks coded 'aspirational_vague' and 2 coded 'structural_process' — the highest structural count in the dataset.

By 2019, the page volume collapsed back to 37 chunks and the explicit demographic terms ('Black,' 'LGBTQ,' 'disability,' 'accessibility') disappeared entirely from the lexicon. Altruism and inclusion z-scores returned to slightly negative territory (−0.21 and −1.21 respectively in 2019). The 2018 inclusion data is anomalous: the z-score drops to −1.53 despite the raw topk mean remaining high, likely because the 2018 crawl captured a German-language subpage ('we pioneer' in German) that diluted the English DEI content — a data artifact worth noting.

sections.heading: Recent Trajectory: Benefits, Representation, and Scaled Belonging
sections.body:
From 2023 onward, the copy shifts toward a workplace-proposition frame: benefits ('average starting pay of $19/hour,' 'health care on day one'), safety metrics ('reduced workplace injury rates by 43% since 2019'), and upskilling ('investing billions of dollars to help our employees and our neighbors prepare for the jobs of the future'). Wellbeing scores, near zero or negative from 2018–2020, climb to z ≈ +1.05 in 2023 and +1.37 in 2026.

DEI language in 2025–26 reframes diversity instrumentally — 'We track the representation of our workforce because we know that diversity helps us build the best possible customer experiences' — rather than as a standalone commitment. The term 'representation' enters the lexicon only in 2025–26, while 'equity' and 'inclusion' drop out after 2024. The register remains 'aspirational_vague' throughout; no year after 2018 registers any 'structural_process' or 'explicit_demographic' chunks. The net picture is a company whose careers copy has moved from a brief, high-volume DEI expansion back toward its durable identity: scale, ownership culture, and customer impact.
